name: Dana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the edge-bander at Brookfield Cabinets. We make kitchen cupboards. The panel saw cuts the boards, and my machine glues the thin strip along the raw edges so you don't see the chipboard. I load the boards, pick the right edge tape for the colour, set the glue temperature, and check every edge with my thumb. You can feel a bad one before you see it. Twelve years there, days, seven till four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a whole kitchen go out on the lorry and knowing every edge on it went through my hands. What wears me out is the lifting, those boards are heavy and I've got a shoulder that complains. My husband Greg has a roofing business, three men and a van, and in the evenings I do his invoices at the kitchen table. So I work two jobs, really, one of them for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, it's a tool, use it where it helps and don't where it doesn't. Greg and I already use it a bit for his quotes. I'd say that at work and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, for Brookfield's sake as much as mine. We've already got a lot of kit, and the small firms have to keep up with the big ones. If AI stays small, everyone stays roughly level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. We've got about three months put by, I'd keep adding a bit. I'd keep using the AI tool for Greg's invoices, it's quicker than my old way. Maybe we'd finally book the trip to see my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to fuss over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for Greg's quotes. How did you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Greg's nephew showed us at Christmas. I was suspicious, but it wrote a quote letter in two minutes that takes me twenty. I check the numbers myself though. I'm not letting a computer tell a customer the wrong price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Brookfield you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big kitchen companies, the ones on the telly. They can buy fancier machines than us. That's business, I don't blame them, you have to compete. Brookfield just has to keep being good.

S0.say: There you go, it's a tool: use it where it helps and don't where it doesn't. Greg and I already use it a bit for his quotes.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, for Brookfield's sake as much as mine. If AI stays small, the small firms and the big ones stay roughly level.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brookfield and keeps adding to the three months of savings. Carries on using AI for Greg's invoices and quotes, and books the trip to see her sister.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to fuss over.
S0.quote: I'm not letting a computer tell a customer the wrong price.
S0.fieldNote: Dana already uses AI carefully for her husband's roofing paperwork and checks every number. She sees competition from bigger firms as fair business, not a grievance. Her concern is as much for the small family-owned firm as for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms have to keep up, and if I owned Brookfield I'd buy the new machines too. But I'd say they should train their own people up, like an apprenticeship, not hire strangers. That's what I'd tell the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the edge-bander gets a robot loader and I go from running one machine to watching three. That could be fine or it could be the end of my job, depending on whether they pick me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brookfield has a setter course, the people who set up the machines for each job. A few have done it. Once I'd seen it pay off for Karen on the panel saw, I'd ask to go on it. I'd also learn the machine software a bit better, the AI help on the screen. And I'd put an extra fifty a week in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if you owned Brookfield you'd buy the machines too. Doesn't that work against you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But it's true. If they don't, the big firms win and we all go. I'd rather work for a firm with robots than a firm that's shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Greg say when you talk about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says come and work for me. He says it every time. I say I'm not doing the books by day and the books by night. But I think about it.

S1.say: Firms have to keep up, and if I owned Brookfield I'd buy the new machines too. But they should train their own people up, like an apprenticeship, not hire strangers.
S1.think: The edge-bander probably gets a robot loader and I go from running one machine to watching three. That could be fine or the end of my job, depending on whether they pick me.
S1.do: Applies for Brookfield's setter course once she sees it pay off for her colleague Karen. Learns more of the machine software and puts an extra 50 a week into savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it on the drive home but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: I'd rather work for a firm with robots than a firm that's shut.
S1.fieldNote: Dana takes the owner's side in public and means it, which is unusual for an operator facing automation. Her preference is for in-house training like an apprenticeship. Greg's standing offer of work in his roofing firm is a quiet second option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and families are going to have to pull together, because the government won't be quick enough. I wouldn't be calling for handouts. I'd say look after your own and your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Brookfield is finished, or near it. Cupboards are boxes, robots can make boxes. And Greg's roofing, if robots can climb roofs in two years, then we've both got a problem at once. I'd be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back straight away, the trip to my sister's goes, no new anything. Try to get the savings from three to five months. I'd go into Greg's business properly, doing the office and chasing payments so he gets paid faster, and he'd take on less. Lean on my parents if we had to, they've offered before. Church too, they're good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years let you do, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much more than tidy up. You can't train for anything in two years if everything's going. I'd use the time to get the money right and keep Greg's business going as long as people still want a person on their roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people want a person on their roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, for a while. The older customers want to see Greg, shake his hand. Mrs Okafor gives him tea every time. But the young ones would book a robot on their phone, I think.

S2.say: It's come too fast and families will have to pull together, because the government won't be quick enough. I wouldn't be calling for handouts, I'd say look after your own and your neighbours.
S2.think: Brookfield is finished or near it, because cupboards are boxes and robots can make boxes. If robots can climb roofs in two years, Greg and I have a problem at the same time.
S2.do: Cancels the trip to her sister and builds savings from three to five months. Moves into Greg's roofing business full-time to run the office and chase payments, and leans on her parents and church if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened, because two years feels like nothing.
S2.quote: Cupboards are boxes, robots can make boxes.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's instinct under pressure is family and church, not the state. She sees both household incomes threatened at once and plans around the roofing business lasting longest. The tea Mrs Okafor makes for Greg is her evidence that some customers will want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for firms to train their people and for families to plan. Get your kids into apprenticeships, keep your skills sharp. That's what I'd say, and I'd probably share some of that on the community page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can do the setter course and maybe stay at Brookfield another three or four years. Then I'd go to Greg's business before Brookfield made the decision for me. I'd rather leave on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the setter course in year one. Keep doing Greg's books in the evenings but properly, get the business on a decent footing. Save, aim for six months. Talk to Emma about her plans, she's fourteen and thinking about hairdressing. That's still a person-to-person job, I'd say go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Lots of lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave on your terms. When would you know it's time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they start bringing in people from the machine supplier to train the setters. That's the sign they're planning to need fewer of us. I'd hand my notice in that month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about going full-time with Greg?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being married to the boss, honestly. We've been together twenty years and never worked together. He'd say I'm bossy. He'd be right.

S3.say: Five years is time for firms to train their people and families to plan. Get your kids into apprenticeships and keep your skills sharp, which I'd share on the community page.
S3.think: Five years means I can do the setter course and maybe stay at Brookfield three or four more years. Then I'd move to Greg's business before Brookfield made the decision for me, on my terms.
S3.do: Takes the setter course in year one and puts Greg's books on a proper footing in the evenings. Saves towards six months, encourages Emma's interest in hairdressing, and plans to leave Brookfield the month the supplier starts training setters.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, with lots of lists.
S3.quote: Being married to the boss, honestly. We've been together twenty years and never worked together.
S3.fieldNote: Dana has a precise exit signal: the day the machine supplier starts training setters. Her plan blends the setter course with a planned move into the family business. The joke about being bossy with Greg shows she feels more in control here than in the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so people should plan and not expect someone else to sort it out. Start a business, learn a trade, look after your family. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years suits us. I'd be fifty-three. I'd go into Greg's business around year three, and we'd build it up while there's still demand. By the time robots are on roofs, the kids are grown and we've got something to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at Brookfield for a couple of years, do the setter course anyway, then join Greg. Put our savings into a second van and another man, grow the business. I'd encourage Luke towards an apprenticeship too, maybe with Greg. And I'd use the AI tools more, for quoting and scheduling, once I'd seen other small firms do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the end, but mostly hopeful. It feels like something we could build together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put savings into a second van. Isn't that a risk if robots come for roofing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But there's ten years. A van pays for itself in three or four if the work's there. And a business with customers is worth selling, even to a robot company. You don't get that from wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That his grandad and his dad worked with their hands and so can he, but he should learn the business side too. The person who knows the customers will last longer than the person who knows the ladder.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, so people should plan and not expect someone else to sort it out. Start a business, learn a trade, look after your family.
S4.think: Ten years suits us, because I'd join Greg's business around year three and build it while there's demand. By the time robots are on roofs, the kids are grown and we've got something to sell.
S4.do: Stays at Brookfield for two years and takes the setter course, then joins Greg's roofing business. Puts savings into a second van and another worker, steers Luke towards an apprenticeship, and adopts AI for quoting and scheduling once other small firms have.
S4.feel: Uneasy about the end but mostly hopeful, as something to build together.
S4.quote: The person who knows the customers will last longer than the person who knows the ladder.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Dana turns the family roofing firm into an investment she could eventually sell. She's open about the risk of the second van but sees business ownership as better than wages. Her advice to Luke mixes hands-on pride with a pragmatic eye on customers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Greg's work and mine could go together and there's no time to build anything. What would help is help for small family firms to buy the new kit and keep their people, and proper apprenticeships, rather than a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women. Half the operators at Brookfield are mums working days so they can do school pick-up. If the job goes, it's not just money, it's the hours that fitted round the kids.

headlineQuote: If the job goes, it's not just money, it's the hours that fitted round the kids.
portrait: Dana Schmidt, 43, runs the edge-bander at Brookfield Cabinets, a kitchen cupboard maker, and does the books for her husband Greg's three-man roofing firm in the evenings. She's pro-business to the point of saying she'd buy the robots herself if she owned the factory, and she prefers family, church and apprenticeships to government help. She uses AI now and then for quotes but checks every number, and she moves once she's seen something work for a colleague. AGI in two years frightens her because both household incomes could go at once, but with ten years she plans to grow Greg's business into something worth selling.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because her job and Greg's roofing work could go at the same time with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small family firms to buy new equipment and keep their staff, and proper apprenticeships rather than a cheque in the post.
